shortlist.title: Deploying liquid intelligence in cancer: Finding answers in our blood
shortlist.abstract: Liquid biopsies are one of the few noninvasive procedures for probing disease at the molecular level. They represent a scalable solution to cancer detection and monitoring by capturing tumor-derived signals from circulating biomolecules such as proteins, DNA, RNA, and metabolites. However, these signals are often sparse, heterogeneous, and shaped by genetics, demographics, and comorbidities. Recent advances in artificial intelligence, especially with multimodal foundation models, have proven capable of extracting signals from noisy, high-dimensional data. Pretraining on large cohorts and integrating complementary modalities may improve sensitivity for tumor signals in blood, though significant clinical and infrastructural barriers remain. This review synthesizes advances in liquid biopsy technologies and artificial intelligence and examines how their convergence can enable enhanced cancer monitoring.

shortlist.title: Cross-species multiomic atlas of the primate basal ganglia
shortlist.abstract: The basal ganglia (BG) are conserved brain regions essential for motor control, learning, emotion, and cognition and are implicated in neurological and psychiatric disease, yet a unified cross-species taxonomy of BG cell types is lacking. We present a multiomic consensus atlas of 1.8 million nuclei from humans, macaques, and marmosets spanning eight BG structures, integrating gene expression, open chromatin, and spatial profiling. Alignment across species and to mouse and human whole-brain atlases identifies 61 homologous cell types conserved over 76 million years. Dorsal-ventral spatial identity is more conserved than D1/D2 receptor or striosome/matrix identity, and striatum (STR) D2 SMYD2-HTR7 spiny projection neurons have distinct molecular, electrophysiological, and morphological features. Cis-regulatory analysis reveals conserved sequence grammars that encode cell identity and inform viral targeting, and cell-type-resolved mapping localizes psychiatric and neurodegenerative risk to specific BG cell populations. This work provides a foundational resource for BG evolution, function, and disease.

shortlist.title: Echoes of the Anthropocene: Noise pollution as a global threat
shortlist.abstract: Anthropogenic noise is a rapidly expanding global pollutant, but its effects across biological levels from individuals to ecosystems remain unquantified. We conducted phylogenetically controlled meta-analyses of 214 experimental studies on 177 aquatic and terrestrial species with ranges that span six continents. Noise altered at least one physiological, developmental, or behavioral trait in 80% of species studied, with declines in fitness and abundance and disruptions of predator-prey interactions. Effects occurred in every habitat, although response mechanisms varied for some traits and species, creating winners and losers. Only multispecies analyses can reveal such species- and ecosystem-level impacts of anthropogenic stressors. Our results establish noise as a novel selection pressure reshaping ecosystem dynamics and as a pervasive stressor requiring soundscape protection alongside habitat conservation.

shortlist.title: Quantitative measurement of viscosity in two-dimensional electron fluids
shortlist.abstract: Electron hydrodynamics is an emerging framework that describes dynamics of interacting electron systems as conventional fluids. Although evidence for hydrodynamic-like transport has been reported in a variety of two-dimensional materials, precise quantitative measurement of the core parameter, electron viscosity, remains challenging. In this work, we demonstrate that magnetoresistance in Corbino-shaped graphene devices offers a simultaneous ohmmeter and viscosometer capability, allowing us to disentangle the individual ohmic and viscous contributions to transport, even near viscous-ohmic crossover. In both monolayer and bilayer graphene, the effective electron-electron scattering rate scales linearly with temperature, deviating markedly from the T 2 dependence expected in conventional Fermi liquids. Instead, it is consistent with a recently identified tomographic fluid regime, theoretically predicted to be generic for two-dimensional electron systems.

shortlist.title: Preventing Malaria Infections and Moving toward Malaria Elimination
shortlist.abstract: Malaria continues to be a major health challenge worldwide, causing an estimated 282 million cases of illness and 610,000 deaths in 2024, predominantly among African children. Despite recent stagnation in the progress of malaria prevention, the landscape is undergoing rapid transformation. This review examines current and emerging approaches to preventing malaria infection and supporting malaria elimination, including vector control, transmission-blocking interventions, chemoprevention, monoclonal antibodies, and vaccines. Next-generation insecticide-treated nets, expanded use of seasonal malaria chemoprevention, and the introduction of RTS,S/AS01 and R21/Matrix-M vaccines are already reshaping control strategies. Looking ahead, long-acting injectable chemoprevention, transmission-blocking medicines and vaccines, and improved surveillance-driven deployment may further accelerate progress. As funding becomes constrained and decision making shifts increasingly to countries where malaria is endemic, effective malaria prevention will depend on locally tailored, integrated combinations of interventions supported by strong surveillance, regulatory capacity, and national leadership.

shortlist.title: Decoding the regulatory programs governing glioblastoma plasticity
shortlist.abstract: Glioblastoma is incurable and resistant to therapy despite genomic stability under treatment 1–8 , suggesting that non-genetic cellular plasticity is a central driver of progression. Whether such plasticity reflects stochastic state switching or is governed by predictable gene regulation has remained unclear 9–13 . Here we introduce scDORI (single-cell deep multi-omic regulatory inference)—a deep-learning framework that infers enhancer-driven gene-regulatory networks at single-cell resolution—and apply it to single-nucleus multiome profiles of more than one million cells from primary glioblastomas. Integrating computational inference with systematic perturbation screens across patient-derived models, we show that a structured regulatory program with an asymmetric interplay of activators and repressors governs cellular plasticity in glioblastoma. The resulting transition landscape is hierarchical and predictable, but permits cross-lineage trajectories that are absent from normal neurodevelopment. Within this landscape, low-plasticity states such as the neuronal-like state are not stable differentiation end points but actively maintained configurations, stabilized by a network of safeguard repressors that silence alternative fates. We identify MYT1L as the dominant member of this network, and show that it binds to and represses master regulators of every alternative state to consolidate neuronal-like identity. MYT1L restricted plasticity even under standard-of-care therapy and suppressed tumour growth and invasion in vivo. Conversely, loss of MYT1L reactivated plasticity and accelerated malignant features, indicating that low-plasticity identity requires continuous repression. These findings reframe malignant cell state stability as a balance between activation and…

shortlist.title: Bouncing singularities in Schwarzschild geometry: A geometric origin of the quasinormal mode convergence region
shortlist.abstract: We show analytically that the convergence of the QNM expansion of the retarded Green's function of the Schwarzschild spacetime is set by a singularity in the complex time plane. The singularity has a simple geometric origin: it is an example of a `bouncing singularity' in the language of AdS/CFT literature, caused by a null geodesic which bounces from the black hole singularity. Our work explains why the QNM convergence region at real times is bounded by null ray which scatters from the gravitational potential at a seemingly unremarkable point (r_* = 0 in the conventions of previous work) -- this ray is the same distance from the origin as the bouncing singularity in the relevant complex plane. The same set of singularities are responsible for an annular region of convergence for the Matsubara mode sum which describes the early time behaviour of the Schwarzschild Green's function for perturbations close to the horizon.

shortlist.title: Obesity management medications: The way forward
shortlist.abstract: Obesity is now widely recognized as a chronic progressive condition. The altered biological mechanisms that cause obesity frequently require long-term treatment, including pharmacotherapies or bariatric surgery. In recent decades, the pathophysiology of obesity has been understood to an extent that obesity management medication (OMM) discovery could be rationally pursued. Advances in defining the regulation of food intake and energy expenditure by molecular communication from peripheral organs to the brain led to the development of OMMs that appear capable of safely achieving scalable and sustained body weight loss. However, side effects, heterogeneous treatment responses, long-term metabolic adaptations, adherence, and other factors may limit the use of existing OMMs and justify the development of additional medications to improve the health of people living with obesity.

shortlist.title: Evolutionary dynamics in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia
shortlist.abstract: Somatic evolution in ageing tissues underlies many cancers 1,2 . However, our quantitative understanding of the rules governing this pre-cancerous evolution remains incomplete. Here we exploit a unique collection of serial blood samples 3 , collected annually for up to a decade and beginning as early as 15 years before diagnosis of acute myeloid leukaemia, to provide a quantitative description of pre-cancerous evolutionary dynamics. Using deep duplex sequencing and evolutionary theory, we quantify the acquisition ages and fitness effects of the key driver events in acute myeloid leukaemia development. The first driver mutations are typically acquired in the first few decades of life, when the blood remains highly polyclonal. These early slow-growing clones subsequently acquire multiple further driver mutations that confer selective advantages up to 100-fold larger than the early drivers. These faster-growing clones harbouring multiple driver mutations can cause complete somatic sweeps of the blood decades before diagnosis, a feature strongly associated with future acute myeloid leukaemia. Our data show that the clonal dynamics of blood are consistent with a set of remarkably simple evolutionary rules that strike a balance between chance and determinism.

shortlist.title: Spatial transcriptomics reveals molecular organization of human and nonhuman primate basal ganglia
shortlist.abstract: The basal ganglia (BG) are interconnected subcortical nuclei with a complex topographical organization that orchestrate goal-directed behaviors and are implicated in neurodegenerative movement disorders. We generated a cellular-resolution spatial transcriptomics atlas of the BG in human, rhesus macaque, and common marmoset, sampling over one million cells in each species. By integrating spatial data with a cross-species consensus single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) cell-type taxonomy, this atlas reveals principles of molecular organization within and across structures. Extensive spatial sampling across the rostral-caudal axis illuminates complex, yet highly stereotyped, multi-axis gene expression gradients superimposed onto discrete compartments of the striatum. Additionally, we identify core-shell organization of the internal globus pallidus. This unified, cross-species spatial transcriptomics atlas will be a foundational resource for characterizing the molecular and functional organization of the BG and their roles in health and disease.

shortlist.title: Anomaly to resource: The Mpemba effect in quantum thermometry
shortlist.abstract: Quantum thermometry provides a key capability for nanoscale devices and quantum technologies, but most existing strategies rely on probes initialized near equilibrium. This equilibrium paradigm imposes intrinsic limitations: sensitivity is tied to long-time thermalization and often cannot be improved in fast, noisy, or nonstationary settings. In contrast, the \textit{Mpemba effect}, the counterintuitive phenomenon where hotter states relax faster than colder ones, has mostly been viewed as a thermodynamic anomaly. Here, we bridge this gap by proving that Mpemba-type inversions generically yield a finite-time enhancement of the quantum Fisher information (QFI) for temperature estimation, thereby converting an anomalous relaxation effect into a concrete metrological resource. Through explicit analyses of two-level and Λ-level probes coupled to bosonic baths, we show that nonequilibrium initializations can transiently outperform both equilibrium strategies and colder states, realizing a \emph{metrological Mpemba effect}. Our results establish anomalous relaxation as a general design principle for nonequilibrium quantum thermometry, enabling ultrafast and nanoscale sensing protocols that exploit, rather than avoid, transient dynamics.

shortlist.title: Intravenous Thrombolysis for Acute Ischemic Stroke — New Directions
shortlist.abstract: In the past 5 years, substantial changes have been made in the use of intravenous thrombolysis (IVT) in patients with acute ischemic stroke. Integrating IVT with endovascular thrombectomy, which improves outcomes in patients with stroke due to large cerebral vessel occlusion, has been a particular challenge. This review discusses the underlying vascular targets for IVT and thrombectomy, the increasing use of tenecteplase instead of alteplase, broadening indications for the use of IVT, and ancillary drugs and dosing methods that may augment the success of IVT.

shortlist.title: Non-halogen aqueous electrolytes for four-electron iodine conversion
shortlist.abstract: Accessing reversible four-electron iodine redox chemistry in aqueous metal–iodine batteries offers a promising route towards high-energy aqueous energy storage, but has conventionally relied on highly concentrated, corrosive halogen-containing electrolytes to stabilize reactive hypervalent iodine cations through interhalogen complexation 1–9 . Here we show a kosmotropic anion–polar anion–nucleophilic species (Nuc) electrolyte framework that harnesses anionic chemistry to coordinate the interfacial microenvironment and molecular interactions, enabling reversible four-electron iodine conversion in halogen-free aqueous electrolytes. Polar anions establish a water-deficient, anion-enriched interfacial microenvironment, whereas kosmotropic anions regulate water–Nuc interactions to increase the availability of Nuc for stabilizing hypervalent iodine cations through Nuc–I + –Nuc halogen bonds. This electrolyte framework is validated across diverse Nuc and in both aqueous Zn–I 2 and Al–I 2 batteries. Moving beyond conventional interhalogen stabilization, these findings establish a distinct electrolyte chemistry framework and represent a mechanistic shift for reversible multi-electron iodine chemistry in aqueous environments.

shortlist.title: Eight New Ultramassive Black Hole Masses Confirm Best Correlation with Galaxy Core Sizes
shortlist.abstract: We analyze black hole (BH) scaling relations at the high-mass end, focusing in particular on the regime of ultramassive black holes, M BH > 10 10 M ⊙ (UMBHs). Building on the new dynamical BH mass measurements presented in our companion paper for a sample of 16 brightest cluster galaxies (BCGs), including eight newly identified UMBHs based on triaxial Schwarzschild models, we investigate the implications of these measurements for BH scaling relations. This first sample of triaxial BH mass determinations increases the number of known UMBHs by a factor of 2 and dramatically increases the constraints for BH mass scaling relations at the high-mass end. We find that BCGs are outliers in the canonical M BH ∝ σ 4−5 relation, while the size of their depleted cores—the central light-deficient region—offers a tighter correlation with M BH with a scatter of 0.22 dex in this mass regime, confirming and extending earlier findings that core size provides a robust proxy at the high-mass end. Our measurements smoothly join the trend already established in previous studies. This also holds for tight correlations between core size and sphere-of-influence radius and core size and core density, which, along with the correlation between M BH and core size, strongly support the BH binary model for the formation of the centers of the most massive galaxies, as the observed core sizes are inconsistent with gravitational-wave recoil predictions and the galaxies display central tangential orbital anisotropy expected from scouring.

shortlist.title: Hyperbolic Large Language Models
shortlist.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success and demonstrated superior performance across various tasks, including natural language processing (NLP), weather forecasting, biological protein folding, text generation, and solving mathematical problems. However, many real-world data exhibit highly non-Euclidean latent hierarchical anatomy, such as protein networks, transportation networks, financial networks, brain networks, and linguistic structures or syntactic trees in natural languages. Effectively learning intrinsic semantic entailment and hierarchical relationships from these raw, unstructured input data using LLMs remains an underexplored area. Due to its effectiveness in modeling tree-like hierarchical structures, hyperbolic geometry—a non-Euclidean space—has rapidly gained popularity as an expressive latent representation space for complex data modeling across domains such as graphs, images, languages, and multimodal data. Here, we provide a comprehensive and contextual exposition of recent advancements in LLMs that leverage hyperbolic geometry as a representation space to enhance semantic representation learning and multiscale reasoning. Specifically, the paper presents a taxonomy of the principal techniques of hyperbolic LLMs (HypLLMs) in terms of four main categories: (1) hyperbolic LLMs through exp/log maps; (2) hyperbolic fine-tuned models; (3) fully hyperbolic LLMs; and (4) hyperbolic state-space models. We also explore crucial potential applications and outline future research directions. A repository of key papers, models, datasets, and code implementations is available at https://github.com/sarangp2402/Hyperbolic-LLM-Models .

shortlist.title: Transcriptomic convergence and the female protective effect in autism
shortlist.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is highly heritable, and mutations in hundreds of genes have been implicated as individually rare causes of ASD 1–3 . Understanding how disruptions to these functionally diverse genes lead to the core features of ASD remains a major challenge 4 . Moreover, ASD is three- to four-fold more common in male than in female individuals 5 , and female autistic people tend to carry more autosomal risk alleles for ASD compared with their male counterparts 6,7 ; however, the biological basis of this ‘female protective effect’ (FPE) has remained unknown 8,9 . Here we show that individual perturbations of 18 ASD genes in human neural progenitor cells converge on shared effects on gene expression, including widespread downregulation of other ASD genes. De novo reconstruction of a gene regulatory network enabled identification of central transcriptional regulators that drive this transcriptomic convergence, including prominent ASD gene CHD8 and candidates including REST . Furthermore, X-linked transcription factor ZFX, which is expressed from both the active and the inactive X chromosomes in female individuals 10 , emerged as a key activator of many ASD genes: we propose that the higher ZFX expression level observed in the female brain can buffer damaging mutations in diverse ASD genes, contributing to the female protective effect. Together, these results show how key gene regulatory networks can become broadly and similarly dysregulated upon disruption of individual ASD genes and provide molecular insight into the female protective effect in ASD.

shortlist.title: On a conjecture of Almgren: area-minimizing submanifolds with fractal singular sets
shortlist.abstract: We construct area-minimizing submanifolds with fractal singular sets on compact Riemannian manifolds. Thus, we settle a conjecture of Almgren, and our answer is sharp dimension-wise. Furthermore, we can prescribe arbitrarily the strata in the Almgren stratification of the singular sets of our area-minimizing submanifolds, and our results hold in the category of integral currents, mod v currents and stable stationary varifolds.

shortlist.title: An Introduction to Computational Fluctuating Hydrodynamics
shortlist.abstract: This short article is an introduction to the theory of fluctuating hydrodynamics (FHD) and the formulation of numerical schemes for the resulting stochastic partial differential equations. The stochastic heat equation (SHE) is derived, and simple finite-volume schemes for its solution are outlined. Numerical results from a Python program (see the supplementary materials ( supplement.pdf [ 196KB])) are shown to be in good agreement with theoretical solutions of the SHE for equilibrium and nonequilibrium systems. Finally, a menagerie of other FHD equations is outlined and suggested instructional exercises are listed.

shortlist.title: diffhydro : Inverse Multiphysics Modeling and Embedded Machine Learning in Astrophysical Flows
shortlist.abstract: We present the extension of the differentiable hydrodynamics code, diffhydro , enabling scalable partial differential equation-constrained inference and integrated hybrid physics–machine learning (ML) models for a wide range of astrophysical applications. New physics additions include radiative heating/cooling, Ornstein–Uhlenbeck–driven turbulence, and self-gravity via multigrid Poisson. We demonstrate good agreement with the Athena++ code on standard validation tests like Sedov–Taylor, Kelvin–Helmholtz, and driven/decaying turbulence. We further introduce a solver-in-the-loop neural corrector that reduces coarse-grid errors during time integration while preserving stability. The addition of custom adjoints facilitates efficient end-to-end gradients and multidevice scaling. We present simulations up to 1024 3 elements, run on distributed GPU systems, and we show gradient-based reconstructions of complex initial conditions in turbulent, and self-gravitating, radiatively cooling flows. The code is written in JAX, and the solver’s modular finite-volume components are compiled by Accelerated Linear Algebra into fused accelerator kernels, delivering high-throughput forward runs and tractable differentiation through long integrations.

shortlist.title: Single-cell analysis of chromatin state and transcriptome in the human basal ganglia
shortlist.abstract: The basal ganglia are central to motor control, learning, emotion, and reward processing, and their dysfunction contributes to many neurological and psychiatric disorders. Here, we generated a single-cell multi-omic atlas of histone modifications and transcriptomes across eight basal ganglia regions from neurotypical human donors. This atlas resolved cell-type- and region-specific landscapes of active and repressive candidate cis -regulatory elements and delineated gene regulatory networks underlying cell identity. We found that the combinatorial expression of homeobox transcription factors provides distinctive molecular descriptors of neuronal cell identities in the basal ganglia. Integration with matched MERFISH spatial transcriptomics further uncovered regional heterogeneity in epigenomic and transcriptional programs. Finally, we used this atlas to interpret noncoding risk variants associated with neuropsychiatric disorders and to construct a deep-learning model that predicts gene regulatory activities and variant effects. Together, this work provides a multimodal regulatory framework for understanding human basal ganglia organization, evolution, and disease genetics.

shortlist.title: High-dimensional families of holomorphic curves and three-dimensional energy surfaces
shortlist.abstract: Let H: R⁴ → R be any smooth function. This article introduces some arguments for extracting dynamical information about the Hamiltonian flow of H from high-dimensional families of closed holomorphic curves. We work in a very general setting, without imposing convexity or contact-type assumptions. For any compact regular level set Y, we prove that the Hamiltonian flow admits an infinite family of pairwise distinct, proper, compact invariant subsets whose union is dense in Y. This is a generalization of the Fish--Hofer theorem, which showed that Y has at least one proper compact invariant subset. We then establish a global Le Calvez--Yoccoz property for almost every compact regular level set Y: any compact invariant subset containing all closed orbits is either equal to Y or is not locally maximal. Next, we prove quantitative versions, in four dimensions, of the celebrated almost-existence theorem for Hamiltonian systems; such questions have been open for general Hamiltonians since the late 1980s. We prove that almost every compact regular level set of H contains at least two closed orbits, a sharp lower bound. Under explicit and C^∞-generic conditions on H, we prove almost-existence of infinitely many closed orbits.

shortlist.title: 100 ± Δ t years of quantum uncertainty: From origins to modern insights
shortlist.abstract: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle is a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, marking a decisive departure from classical physics. Conceived almost a century ago through a thought experiment showing that measuring an electron's position inevitably disturbs its momentum, it began as a deceptively simple idea that sparked countless studies and grew into the rich research field it is today. This review traces its development into a spectrum of mathematical formulations -- known as uncertainty relations -- and explores their interconnections and wide-ranging applications. We highlight its central role in quantum metrology, where it underpins strategies for extracting information from quantum systems with ever-increasing precision, and its links to multiparameter estimation and squeezed states. This review, dedicated to the centenary of the uncertainty principle, reflects on how it has deepened our understanding of quantum theory and driven practical advances, and looks ahead to a century poised for further surprising and transformative discoveries.

shortlist.title: Inverse Design of Inorganic Compounds with Generative AI
shortlist.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
shortlist.abstract: Machine learning is revolutionizing chemistry. Beyond the value of predictive models accelerating virtual screening, generative AI aims at enabling inverse design, reversing the compound-to-property prediction paradigm into property-to-compound generation. Chemists now have access to a rich AI toolbox for organic chemistry, including drug discovery. However, the application of these methods to inorganic compounds remains limited by the challenges posed by their intrinsic nature. This perspective analyzes how these challenges have been addressed, considering widely diverse systems ranging from molecules to crystals, including transition metal complexes and microporous materials. The analysis focuses on how generative AI methods have evolved toward data-representation-model pipelines that address the full complexity of inorganic compounds, including their chemical composition, geometry, symmetry, and electronic structure. Future directions, like benchmark standardization and the development of synthesizability metrics, are also discussed.

shortlist.title: Reconciling Discrete-Time Mixed Policies and Continuous-Time Relaxed Controls in Reinforcement Learning and Stochastic Control
shortlist.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is currently one of the most prominent methods for optimizing dynamical systems, with breakthrough results across various fields. The framework is based on the concept of a Markov decision process (MDP), leading to a discrete-time optimal control problem. In the RL literature, such problems are typically formulated and solved using mixed policies, from which random actions are sampled at each time step. Recently, part of the optimal control community has begun investigating continuous-time versions of RL algorithms, replacing MDPs with continuous-time stochastic processes governed by relaxed controls and asserting a full analogy between the two formulations. In this work, we examine the limitations of this analogy and rigorously establish a connection between the two problems in the case where only the drift term of the continuous-time model is controlled. We prove strong convergence of the RL implementation of mixed strategies as the time discretization mesh tends to zero. We also discuss the technical challenges posed by the possible presence of control in the diffusion component of the state.

shortlist.title: Colloquium: Semi-Dirac fermions in quantum matter
shortlist.abstract: This article reviews the recent progress on the subject of semi-Dirac fermions, two dimensional quasiparticles that disperse quadratically, as Galilean invariant particles, or linearly, as massless relativistic particles, depending on their direction of motion. These particles exist at a phase boundary set by the continuous change in the connectivity of Fermi surfaces, known as topological Lifshitz transitions. The basic properties and the current experimental evidence of the existence of these particles in both synthetic lattices and quantum materials are presented. The many-body problem of semi-Dirac fermions is discussed from a theoretical perspective with an eye to physical observables of relevance to experiments.

shortlist.title: Ambipolar Electrochemical Doping of CsPbBr 3 Nanocrystals
shortlist.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
shortlist.abstract: Electronic doping underpins many semiconductor applications but has remained elusive for lead halide perovskite nanocrystals because their high density and low formation energy of defects easily compensate introduced dopants. Here, we use electrochemical doping as a strategy to avoid doping compensation. Electrochemical injection of electrons or holes into the nanocrystal is compensated by surface-adsorbed electrolyte counterions, therefore not compromising crystal structure. We accomplished ambipolar (n- and p-type) doped CsPbBr3 nanocrystals with charge carrier concentrations ranging from intrinsic up to 4.8 × 1017 cm–3 (corresponding to 0.25 charges per nanocrystal). We show that electrochemical doping is reversible and stable at these free carrier concentrations. The extent of doping and stability are enabled by the use of lecithin, a zwitterionic ligand that strongly binds to the surface of the CsPbBr3 nanocrystals while still allowing ion and electron transfer. Lecithin stabilizes the surface atoms by shifting the potentials for Pb2+ reduction and Br– oxidation outside of the bandgap. The inferred surface-chemistry design rules for stable electrochemical doping can also serve as a guideline for developing CsPbBr3 nanocrystals stable under high free-carrier concentrations in optoelectronic devices, such as light-emitting diodes or electronically triggered quantum light sources.

shortlist.title: Systemic Cyber Risk: Linking Measurement, Market Incentives, and Policy
shortlist.abstract: Many firms and sectors within the global economy heavily depend on a common set of critical technology products and software services, thereby consolidating risk across a small number of potential failure points. The widespread reliance on a limited set of products and services has given rise to many single points of system vulnerability. Such concentration of risk amplifies the potential fallout from security breaches, especially since attackers have strong incentives to attack such products and services. Despite the abundance of tools available to organizations and consumers for safeguarding their data against loss or compromise, advancements in individual defense measures have been more than counterbalanced by an increased susceptibility to systemic events. In this paper, we apply economic principles to the rising danger of systemic cyber risks. The paper is organized around four central economic lessons and uses case studies, new data, and policy discussion to develop and support them.

shortlist.title: Optical Access to a Molecular Nuclear-Spin Register in Catalytically Relevant Palladium(I) Complexes
shortlist.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
shortlist.abstract: Paramagnetic metal complexes are powerful tools in chemical catalysis and, increasingly, quantum information science, positioning them as ideal tools for quantum sensing within reactions themselves. However, this application requires an interface between spins and light in chemically relevant platforms. Here, we demonstrate that circularly polarized light can generate electron spin coherence in low-symmetry, catalytically relevant Pd(I) complexes. By measuring ultrafast changes in optical polarization with time-resolved Faraday rotation, we optically detect coherent superhyperfine interaction between the Pd(I)-centered electron spin and adjacent 31P nuclei from the ligand at ambient temperature in solution. The electronic origins of this behavior are attributed to excited-state orbital angular momentum through combined spectroscopic and computational analysis, and the optically measured coherence is benchmarked against pulsed electron paramagnetic resonance. Spin polarization is coherently exchanged between the electron spin and initially incoherent nuclear spins, constituting a rare example of optical access to a nuclear spin register in an ambient-temperature, solution-phase molecular system. Both reactivity and quantum spin function are mediated by the bisphosphine ligand; taken together with in situ detection of coherent Pd(I) spin dynamics directly in reaction mixtures, this work moves molecular qubits toward quantum sensing in chemical reactions.

shortlist.title: Porphyrin-Driven Redox Tuning in Structurally Defined De Novo Heme Proteins
shortlist.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
shortlist.abstract: Designing redox proteins with predictable and tunable electron transfer properties is a major goal in de novo bioenergetics. Here we show that replacing heme B with a series of structurally conservative non-natural metalloporphyrins enables broad modulation of redox potentials over 400 mV in the de novo designed monoheme m4D2 and diheme 4D2 T19D. The non-natural porphyrins bind with high affinity and do not compromise either the heme binding site or global protein structure, as evidenced by X-ray crystallography and NMR spectroscopy. We also report the native-like NMR structure of m4D2 loaded with the non-natural and symmetric iron 2,4-dimethyldeuteroporphyrin IX, confirming our modular approach to tetrahelical redox protein design. This work establishes a versatile platform for constructing tunable electron carriers for engineered bioenergetic pathways and bioelectronic applications.

shortlist.title: Channeled Attention and Stable Errors
shortlist.abstract: People persist in mistaken beliefs even in settings with high stakes, abundant data, and repeated opportunities to learn—settings where standard arguments imply they should correct their errors. We develop an attention-based framework for understanding why errors persist. When a person channels his attention through the lens of his potentially misspecified model, exposure to data is not the same as tracking the statistics necessary to tell him his model is wrong. A model is attentionally stable when the data the person deems relevant will, in the long run, fail to make the model look implausible. Models that erroneously rule things out—e.g., beliefs that a variable doesn’t matter or that a distinction doesn’t exist—tend to be attentionally stable because they divert attention away from data that would refute the models. Conversely, models that erroneously rule things in are less likely to be stable. Whether an error is discovered depends on the structure of the decision problem but is not tightly linked to its level of harm; arbitrarily costly errors can persist while trivially inexpensive ones may be detected. Nevertheless, no error is robust both to changes in the decision environment and to shocks that expand attention: every channeled-attention error is vulnerable to some perturbation that would reveal it. We use the framework to analyze the stability of psychological biases and empirical misconceptions, as well as to explain why fresh eyes catch mistakes, why people use overly coarse rather than overly fine categorizations, and why people recognize errors in others that they miss in themselves.

shortlist.title: TAVR in Patients with Moderate Aortic Stenosis with At-Risk Features
shortlist.abstract: BACKGROUND: For patients with moderate aortic stenosis, current guidelines recommend clinical surveillance with echocardiographic assessment every 1 or 2 years. Whether transcatheter aortic-valve replacement (TAVR) will improve outcomes in these patients remains unknown. METHODS: We conducted an international, open-label, randomized trial to evaluate whether TAVR will result in better outcomes than clinical surveillance among patients with moderate aortic stenosis with at least one at-risk feature (i.e., a symptom or structural or functional abnormality that has been shown to be associated with faster disease progression or adverse cardiovascular outcomes). The patients were assigned in a 1:1 ratio to undergo transfemoral TAVR with a balloon-expandable valve or clinical surveillance. The primary effectiveness end point was a composite of death from any cause or a heart-failure event with or without hospitalization at 2 years. Superiority testing was performed in the intention-to-treat population. RESULTS: , and the mean aortic-valve peak velocity was 3.3 m per second. At 2 years, the Kaplan-Meier estimate of the percentage of patients with a primary effectiveness end-point event was 16.7% in the TAVR group and 23.9% in the clinical-surveillance group (risk difference, -7.2 percentage points; 95% confidence interval, -13.1 to -1.3; P = 0.02 for superiority). METHODS: In two double-blind, placebo-controlled trials, 757 adults with severe hypertriglyceridemia were randomly assigned in a 2:1 ratio to receive plozasiran (25 mg) or placebo at baseline and at months 3, 6, and 9. A higher dietary protein intake preserves fat-free mass during energy restriction-induced weight loss in individuals with overweight or obesity: a systematic review, meta-analysis, and meta-regression
shortlist.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
shortlist.abstract: Background A higher dietary protein intake is often advocated to preserve fat-free mass during energy restriction-induced weight loss, yet the magnitude of effect in previous meta-analyses is highly variable. Objectives We aimed to determine the effects of a higher dietary protein intake on body composition during energy restriction-induced weight loss in individuals with overweight or obesity, with consideration for exercise, age, and protein difference. Methods We performed a systematic review to identify randomized controlled trials implementing higher or normal protein intakes alongside energy restriction-induced weight loss in individuals with overweight or obesity. Random-effects meta-analyses {mean difference [MD] [95% confidence intervals (CI)]} were performed for changes in fat-free mass and fat mass, respectively. Subgroup meta-analysis and meta-regression were performed to investigate potential modifiers of protein intake on fat-free mass changes. Results Thirty-three studies ( n = 2135) were included. A higher protein intake compared with a normal protein intake (mean ± standard deviation: 0.79 ± 0.11 compared with 1.25 ± 0.27 g⋅kg –1 ⋅d –1 ) preserved fat-free mass [MD (95% CI): 0.26 (0.04, 0.48) kg, P = 0.02, I 2 = 61%] and promoted greater fat mass loss [MD (95% CI): −0.69 (−0.95, −0.42) kg, P < 0.01, I 2 = 25%]. Subgroup meta-analysis found no effect of exercise compared with no exercise on fat-free mass ( P = 0.12). Exploratory analysis demonstrated exercise augmented fat-free mass preservation with a higher protein intake [MD (95% CI): 0.49 (0.14, 0.83) kg, P < 0.01]. However, this effect was only significant in younger (<60 y) adults [MD (95% CI): 0.60 (0.12, 1.09) kg, P = 0.01] and not in older (≥60 y) adults [MD (95% CI): 0.34 (−0.19, 0.87) kg, P…

shortlist.title: Named Reactions under Mechanochemical Conditions: A Critical Survey
shortlist.abstract: Mechanochemistry has progressed from a niche interest to a core method for solvent-free synthesis, providing sustainable and mechanistically unique alternatives to traditional solution-based chemistry. When controlled impact, shear, or vibrational energy is applied under solvent-free or solvent-lean conditions, reactions are promoted within dynamically renewed interfacial regions, revealing new patterns of selectivity, energy efficiency, and process design. This review surveys the historical development, fundamental principles, and analytical frameworks of mechanochemistry, together with an extensive compilation of named organic reactions conducted under mechanochemical conditions. By comparing mechanochemical reactions with their solution-phase counterparts, this review clarifies how stress-induced activation, microsolvation (η control), and auxiliary-mediated interfaces influence reaction kinetics, selectivity, and scalability. Emerging platforms, such as twin-screw extrusion (TSE), resonant acoustic mixing (RAM), and bead mills, extend these advantages toward scale-up and, in the case of TSE, continuous manufacturing, bridging laboratory-scale discoveries and industrial applications. Mechanochemistry functions both as a practical enabling platform and as a conceptual framework for Green Chemistry, embracing atom economy, solvent reduction, and operational safety within a unified solid-state synthetic framework.

shortlist.title: When Insurers Exit: Climate Losses, Fragile Insurers, and Mortgage Markets
shortlist.abstract: This paper uses a range of natural experiments to show how mispricing of climate risk in mortgages and property insurance creates large taxpayer exposures and leads to excess credit flows to risky areas. Our central finding is that the government-sponsored enterprises’ (GSEs) policies for evaluating property insurers are a crucial source of this mispricing. We assemble a comprehensive new dataset on both mortgages and insurance to analyze these dynamics in Florida from 2009-2018. We begin by documenting a breakdown in the quality of insurance provision, with new under-capitalized and under-diversified insurers dominating insurance markets. These fragile insurers have high rates of insolvency, which we show causally increases mortgage defaults after natural disasters. We find that the GSEs’ reliance on third-party ratings of insurers leads them to accept insurance from companies at high risk of insolvency without pricing for it. This creates large taxpayer exposures, with an estimated 25% of the GSEs’ expected losses in Florida coming from insurance fragility. Most starkly, we show that private lenders strategically respond to the GSE mispricing. Mortgage denial rates are sensitive to insurance quality in the jumbo segment where loans are retained, but not in the conforming segment where loans are offloaded to the GSEs. This suggests that, all else equal, fewer conforming mortgages would have been originated if lenders screened insurance fragility as they do in jumbos.

shortlist.title: Breathlessness mechanisms, measurement, and management in adults: evidence update on behalf of The Dyspnoea Society
shortlist.abstract: Breathlessness affects an estimated 40% of adults living with chronic disease, with substantial consequences for individuals, carers, and health-care systems. This Dyspnoea Society Research Statement, developed for researchers, clinicians, and adults living with or caring for someone with breathlessness, provides a state-of-the-art synthesis of recent advances in chronic breathlessness mechanisms, measurement, and management, and outlines a research agenda for the next decade. Key advancements include establishment of neural respiratory drive as a mechanistic contributor to exertional breathlessness; neuroimaging evidence that breathlessness arises from integration of peripheral and central processes within a dynamic brain network involving sensorimotor and cognitive-affective regions, supporting behavioural and psychosocial interventions; and improved measurement through responsive multidimensional instruments and approaches to quantify symptom abnormality relative to physical activity. Evidence supports early use of low-risk, non-pharmacological interventions for management of breathlessness, whereas evidence for pharmacological therapies is limited in most situations. Health-care redesign, including symptom-focused diagnostic pathways, integrated care models, and disease-agnostic breathlessness services, might help to improve patient outcomes while reducing health-care costs.

shortlist.title: "If we don't act now, someone will die" : temporal riskwork in action
shortlist.abstract: In this ethnographic study, we develop the concept of temporal riskwork -- actions taken to alter the temporal dynamics of risk -- by examining how riskworkers navigated situations of multiple dynamically evolving risks under severe time constraints. In such contexts, decisions about how and when to act are critically interdependent and made with attention to assessing urgencies, priorities and volatility of risk. Our study revealed how risk can present both synchronic and diachronic competing temporal demands, requiring temporally complex riskwork. We studied a mental health crisis team where actors collectively responded to clients’ urgent, often accelerating risks in high-stakes, time-pressured environments. We contribute to the literature by developing a model of temporal riskwork that explains how actors can collectively manage a set of ongoing risks by engaging in two connected temporal processes: decelerating synchronic risk momenta and redirecting diachronic risk trajectories. More generally, our model explains how riskworkers can collectively manage the temporal complexity of multiple concurrent risks, integrating their assessments and actions in complex, dynamic contexts.

shortlist.title: In Praise of the Bayesian Bootstrap
shortlist.abstract: The key takeaways from this article will be the following: (i) Anytime you can bootstrap, you should! (ii) Use the Bayesian bootstrap instead of the nonparametric bootstrap. (iii) If the bootstrap distribution looks different from the “theoretical” (usually, normal) distribution, don’t (only) report a point estimate and standard error. (iv) Instead (or in addition), report the bootstrap distribution with a plot if you have space for it or an interval if you don’t. (v) Give the Bayesian bootstrap a Bayesian interpretation. (vi) You can use a bootstrap even with (multiway) clustering.

shortlist.title: Reframing disease elimination: an update from the Lancet Commission on chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
shortlist.abstract: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, with increasing global burden driven by population growth and ageing, persistent harmful exposures, and substantial health inequities. The Lancet Commission on COPD articulated an ambitious vision for disease elimination with prevention, early detection, and intervention. This Review revisits that vision, assesses progress since 2022, and calls for a broader commitment to lifelong lung health as an update of the Commission. Across seven sections, this Review advances a unified framework integrating the biology of lung development and ageing, precision medicine, patient-centred outcomes, and regulatory reform. COPD is not a single, uniform disease; rather, a biologically complex condition shaped by genetic, developmental, environmental, infectious, and behavioural factors across the entire life course. Effective prevention and care should therefore move beyond the detection and treatment of late physiological impairment toward earlier disease recognition, biological stratification, and interventions to preserve lung health, reduce symptoms, and prevent morbidity and premature mortality. The Review charts a path from reactive, late-stage management toward proactive, equitable, precision-based prevention and care. The central premise is unequivocal: the global burden of COPD can be substantially reduced. Success should be measured not only by gains in lung function and survival but also by improvements in daily functioning, quality of life, and wellbeing. In this expanded vision, COPD is no longer viewed solely as a chronic disease to be managed but as a preventable and modifiable condition within a broader commitment to lifelong lung health.

shortlist.title: Trends in the burden of diseases and their associations with multidimensional development among children and adolescents in China from 2000 to 2019: a retrospective analysis of a nationwide, repeated, cross-sectional survey
shortlist.abstract: BACKGROUND: Rapid social progress has transformed the health profile of Chinese children and adolescents, with declining diseases associated with poverty and rising diseases associated with wealth. This study aims to describe national trends in disease transitions and examine their associations with multidimensional provincial development. METHODS: In this retrospective study, we analysed data from the 2000, 2005, 2010, 2014, and 2019 waves of the nationwide, repeated, cross-sectional Chinese National Surveys on Students' Constitution and Health in Han Chinese children and adolescents aged 7-18 years from 30 provinces in mainland China. The survey used a multistage, stratified, cluster-sampling design with balanced distributions by age, sex, and residence (urban vs rural). Collected data were prevalences of diseases associated with wealth and development (overweight and obesity, dental caries, and visual impairment) and their coexistence (multimorbidity associated with wealth) in addition to diseases associated with poverty (undernutrition, anaemia, and Ascaris infestation), and their coexistence (multimorbidity associated with poverty). We integrated 13 provincial indicators reflecting economic, social, environmental, infrastructure, and innovation development to construct a Multidimensional Equality Development Index (MEDI) using an entropy method. To examine national trends in disease transitions and their associations with multidimensional development we used mixed-effects logistic regression and restricted cubic splines. Population-attributable fractions were estimated to describe how development domains related to disease patterns. FINDINGS: The study included 1 085 072 participants across five survey waves. shortlist.title: Private Credit, Balance Sheets, and Financial Stability
shortlist.abstract: Private credit has become an important source of business financing, raising questions about financial stability. We examine these questions using comprehensive fund- and asset-level data on private credit funds, the dominant form of private credit. Four facts emerge. First, private credit funds are primarily equity financed, with equity accounting for 65–80 percent of assets, compared with about 10 percent for US banks. Second, they engage in little maturity transformation: Fund lives span eight to twelve years, while underlying loans typically mature within two to four years. Third, portfolios are diversified across industries, geographies, and credit strategies. Fourth, equity investors have earned average net annualized returns of about 10 percent after fees, with equity cushions historically absorbing losses before creditors. These findings suggest that private credit funds do not currently replicate balance-sheet structures associated with banking fragility. We conclude by discussing potential vulnerabilities related to liquidity provision, valuation contagion, and loss transmission through investor balance sheets.

shortlist.title: Can Government Support for Innovation Create the Next Silicon Valley?
shortlist.abstract: Can government support for innovation create the next Silicon Valley? We examine what public research and development can and cannot do to foster regional knowledge hubs. The historical record suggests that many successful hubs owe their origins partly to serendipity and favorable initial conditions. We then review causal evidence from universities, changes in intellectual property rules, new research institutions, wartime R&D, and the space race. Public R&D can raise local innovation, employment, and income, but the effects are heterogeneous, often modest relative to cost, and may partly reflect the relocation of firms and skilled workers from elsewhere. The evidence suggests a central role for complementary local inputs, including entrepreneurs, risk capital, skilled labor, firms, and institutions. Public R&D can help build a hub, but is unlikely to create one on its own.

shortlist.title: Abstract 13530: Factor XI/XIa Inhibitors for Secondary Prevention After Non-Cardioembolic Ischemic Stroke and High-Risk Transient Ischemic Attack: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
shortlist.abstract: Background: Factor XI/Xia inhibitors have gained attention as an innovative anticoagulant strategy which may reduce thrombosis without substantially impairing hemostasis. Their role in secondary prevention following non-cardioembolic stroke and high-risk transient ischemic attack (TIA) remains uncertain. We conducted an updated systematic review and meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trial (RCTs) assessing the efficacy and safety of factor XI/Xia inhibition in patient with these conditions. Research Question: Does treatment with factor XI/XIa inhibitors improve clinical outcomes while minimizing bleeding complications compared with conventional therapy in patients with non-cardioembolic stroke or high-risk TIA? Methods: A thorough search was performed on PubMed, Scopus, Embase, ClinicalTrials.gov and the Cochrane library from inception until May 2025 comparing Factor XI/XIa inhibitors, primarily asundexian and milvexian, with placebo or standard antithrombotic therapy in patients with non-cardioembolic ischemic stroke or high-risk TIA. Pooled Risk Ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were computed using random-effects models. Results: Five RCTs involving 18,603 participants were included. Factor XI/XIa inhibitors were associated with a significant reduction in symptomatic ischemic stroke compared with control therapy (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.68-0.86; p<0.00001; I 2 =0%). No significant differences were observed for the composite of symptomatic ischemic stroke and covert infarction (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.87-1.18; p=0.89; I 2 =0%) or the composite of symptomatic ischemic stroke and TIA (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.61-1.01; p=0.06; I 2 =0%). shortlist.title: The commutativity problem for effective varieties of formal series, and applications
shortlist.abstract: A formal series in noncommuting variables Σ over the rationals is a mapping Σ * → Q from the free monoid generated by Σ to the rationals. We say that it is commutative if the output does not depend on the order of the symbols in the input. The commutativity problem for a class of series takes as input a (finite presentation of) a series from the class and amounts to establishing whether it is commutative. This is a very natural, albeit nontrivial problem, which has not been considered before from an algorithmic perspective. We show that commutativity is decidable for all classes of series that constitute a so-called effective prevariety , a notion generalising Reutenauer’s varieties of formal series. For example, the class of rational series , introduced by Schützenberger in the 1960’s, is well-known to be an effective (pre)variety, and thus commutativity is decidable for it. In order to showcase the applicability of our result, we consider classes of formal series generalising the rational ones. We consider polynomial automata , shuffle automata , and infiltration automata , and we show that each of these models recognises an effective prevariety of formal series. Consequently, their commutativity problem is decidable, which is a novel result. We find it remarkable that commutativity can be decided in a uniform way for such disparate computation models. Finally, we present applications of commutativity outside the theory of formal series. We show that we can decide solvability in sequences and in power series for restricted classes of algebraic difference and differential equations, for which such problems are undecidable in full generality. Thanks to this, we can prove that the syntaxes of multivariate polynomial recursive sequences and of constructible…

shortlist.title: Abstract 15126: Elective Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump Ranks Highest for Survival in High-Risk Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Bayesian Network Meta-Analysis of Randomized Trials
shortlist.abstract: Background: The optimal mechanical circulatory support strategy for patients undergoing high-risk percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) remains uncertain. Randomized trials evaluating elective intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP), Impella, and standard care have reported conflicting results and have not been synthesized within a unified comparative framework. Research Question/Hypothesis: We evaluated the comparative efficacy and safety of elective IABP, Impella, and standard care in planned high-risk PCI. Methods: We systematically identified randomized controlled trials enrolling patients with severe left ventricular dysfunction undergoing planned high-risk PCI. A Bayesian random-effects network meta-analysis compared elective IABP, Impella, and standard care. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included periprocedural myocardial injury, major bleeding, vascular complications, spontaneous myocardial infarction, and stroke. Results: Three randomized trials (BCIS-1, PROTECT II, and CHIP-BCIS3) comprising 1,053 patients formed a closed triangular evidence network. Model convergence was excellent (all R̂<1.01), with low estimated between-study heterogeneity (posterior median τ=0.346). For all-cause mortality, elective IABP demonstrated the most favorable treatment profile. Compared with standard care, IABP was associated with a 40% reduction in mortality odds (OR 0.60, 95% CrI 0.24-1.31) and an 89.7% posterior probability of benefit. This signal remained consistent across prespecified sensitivity analyses, including long-term follow-up data (OR 0.64, 95% CrI 0.29-1.30; probability of benefit 91.4%). shortlist.title: Harnessing Contact Electrification and Static Charge for Chemical Reactions: Fundamentals and Applications of Contact Electrocatalysis
shortlist.abstract: The chemical industry is the largest industrial energy consumer and the third-largest emitter of CO2 globally. Despite efforts to enhance energy efficiency, many chemical reactions still require significant external energy due to fundamental thermodynamic barriers. Thus, transitioning to a sustainable chemical industry requires new renewable energy or catalytic technologies that reduce energy demand. In catalytic systems, flowing liquids, moving parts, and gas separation mean local static charge is often generated on the nanoscale. This review explores the static charge formation at solid–solid, solid–liquid, and solid–gas interfaces, such as those that occur in catalytic reactions, and then extends this discussion to a deeper focus on how these generated static charges can be used for catalysis, including electrostatic catalysis, static charge electrochemistry, and contact electrocatalysis (CEC). CEC, where motion-induced charge separation leads to local static charge formation, is then specifically examined, exploring why and how it has emerged as an exciting tool to enable these green chemical transformations. The focus is to highlight the most recent developments in CEC, with mechanistic interpretation, factors that affect CEC performance, and emerging applications, and to provide outlook and guidance for the field─specifically highlighting the need to build structure–property relationships for CEC performance and static charge formation for target chemical reactions.

shortlist.title: Transition-Metal-Catalyzed Multicomponent Cycloadditions
shortlist.abstract: Transition-metal-catalyzed multicomponent cycloadditions provide a powerful strategy for constructing complex cyclic frameworks from simple unsaturated building blocks with high atom and step efficiencies. This Review highlights the progress made in transition-metal-catalyzed multicomponent cycloadditions based on the size of the cyclic products formed. First, reactions that construct five-membered rings, including [2 + 2 + 1], [3 + 1 + 1], and [2 + 1 + 1 + 1] cycloadditions, are discussed with an emphasis on key reactive intermediates, such as carbon monoxide, vinylidenes, carbenoids, and nitrenes. Next, six-membered-ring-forming processes, particularly [2 + 2 + 2], [3 + 2 + 1], [4 + 1 + 1], and [2 + 1 + 2 + 1] cycloadditions, are described, highlighting combinations of alkynes, alkenes, and heteroatom-containing components. The Review then covers strategies for constructing seven-membered rings via [3 + 2 + 2] and [4 + 2 + 1] cycloadditions. Finally, emerging methods that enable the formation of eight- and nine-membered rings through higher-order multicomponent cycloadditions are described. This Review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the conceptual framework, mechanistic principles, and synthetic possibilities of transition-metal-catalyzed multicomponent cycloadditions by organizing them according to ring size and cycloaddition components.

shortlist.title: Efficient and accurate mixed model association tool for single-cell eQTL analysis
shortlist.abstract: Genetic effects on gene expression often vary across cell types, motivating expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) mapping in single-cell RNA sequencing data. Existing approaches generally aggregate expression across cells, use Gaussian models poorly suited to read counts or do not scale. Here we show that SAIGE-QTL, a Poisson mixed model that directly models single-cell read counts, enables calibrated and computationally scalable eQTL mapping while accounting for donor-level and cell-level covariates and unequal numbers of cells per donor. In simulations and three single-cell datasets, SAIGE-QTL improved statistical efficiency and discovery of genes with significant eQTLs (eGenes) relative to pseudobulk methods and produced results consistent with existing single-cell models at substantially lower computational cost. In 1.2 million immune cells, SAIGE-QTL identified 48.8% more eGenes than pseudobulk analysis. SAIGE-QTL further enabled genome-wide trans-eQTL mapping and rare variant set-based testing, identifying rare variant associations independent of common eQTL signals. SAIGE-QTL therefore expands single-cell eQTL discovery across common, rare and trans-acting genetic variation.

shortlist.title: Diffusion Models for Small-Molecule Design
shortlist.abstract: Diffusion models (DMs) have emerged as a class of generative models for controllable small-molecule design in drug discovery capable of progressively transforming noisy or partially specified molecular states into candidate structures under structural, geometric, and property constraints. This Review provides a comprehensive overview of the methodological foundations and representative applications of diffusion-based molecular generation, emphasizing the alignment among molecular representations, generative dynamics, controllable design, and evaluation and validation. Particular attention is given to recent advances in property- and structure-guided generation, target-aware and fragment-based design, multiobjective optimization, and synthesis-aware generation. We also discuss the roles of data sets, computational evaluation, and prospective experiments in assessing the chemical and biological relevance of generated molecules. By organizing these developments within a unified conceptual framework, we provide computational chemists and drug discovery researchers with a structured roadmap that balances the mathematical rigor with chemical intuition. Throughout, we highlight current methodological limitations and unresolved challenges and conclude with future directions toward chemically credible and experimentally grounded molecular design. To facilitate navigation of this rapidly evolving field, we introduce an interactive companion platform (https://diffsmd.scbdd.com) that provides a curated, continuously updated repository of model architectures and visualizations.

shortlist.title: Participatory Budgeting in Public Health: Promise, Evidence, Challenges, and Opportunities
shortlist.abstract: Participatory budgeting (PB) is a deliberative decision-making process that invites community participation to direct spending for a defined portion of public budgets. Originating in Brazil in the 1980s, PB has since diffused across the globe, including several hundred cases in the United States and Canada alone. PB programs vary but are generally characterized by five core principles: voice, vote, social inclusion, social justice, and oversight. Research on PB shows promising though moderate associations with improved population health outcomes, including infant mortality reductions and health and sanitation spending increases. Despite PB's conceptual alignment with many public health values, adoption of PB by US public health agencies remains limited, constrained by categorical funding requirements, small discretionary budgets, and a polarized sociopolitical environment. This article reviews PB's conceptual foundations, evidence base, and real-world applications before examining structural and political challenges and opportunities for PB as a means to improve the public's health.

shortlist.title: Proximal redox coupling enables oxidation damping for stable water electrolysis
shortlist.abstract: The design of atomically precise catalysts requires strategies that regulate their electronic and structural dynamics under operating conditions. While conventional doping can effectively tune bulk materials, it translates poorly to single-atom catalysts (SACs), in which isolated atoms lack extended coordination and are prone to oxidative instability. Here we design atomically dispersed Ru−O−Cr motifs that enable oxidation damping during acidic oxygen evolution. In situ X-ray absorption spectroscopy shows attenuated Ru oxidation synchronized with anticorrelated and partially reversible Cr redox evolution, consistent with proximity-dependent redox coupling. This buffered redox response is accompanied by bounded and partially reversible changes in the local metal−oxygen coordination environment. These coupled dynamics support proximity-coupled Ru−O−Cr redox units, enabling a 55.7-fold increased resistance against oxidation-induced Ru dissolution compared with conventional SACs. In proton exchange membrane water electrolysis, catalysts incorporating proximal Ru−O−Cr configurations exhibit degradation rates that are 6.8-fold and 14.4-fold lower than those of Ru SACs and commercial RuO2, respectively, at 1 A cm−2. These results suggest proximal oxidation damping as a potential design principle for stabilizing atomically precise electrocatalysts. Single-atom catalysts can mitigate reliance on scarce noble metals, but isolated sites can be fragile. Here a catalyst with proximal Ru−O−Cr motifs is fabricated that demonstrates proximal oxidation damping where the Cr neighbour buffers Ru overoxidation, improving stability for acidic oxygen evolution.

shortlist.title: Optimal learning of quantum channels in diamond distance
shortlist.abstract: The evolution of quantum states can be described by quantum channels. The task of estimating an unknown quantum channel, known as process tomography, is a central problem in quantum information theory. A long-standing open question is how many uses of an unknown channel are required to learn it to a precision quantified by the standard metric for distinguishing quantum processes, known as the diamond distance. Here we address this by establishing the query complexity of channel tomography with optimal dependence on the dimensions of the input and output spaces and the channel’s Kraus rank at any fixed constant accuracy in diamond distance. We design an algorithm that establishes an upper bound and prove a matching lower bound for learning a channel to the given accuracy. Our algorithm follows the strategy of performing optimal tomography on the Choi-state representation of the process, and we show that channel tomography can be reduced to the well-studied problem of pure-state tomography. As channels subsume states, unitaries and measurements as special cases, our protocol provides a unified framework for tomography of these tasks.

A purification channel then maps these Choi-state copies to copies of a random purification |Φ_c⟩ , which are learned using a sample-optimal pure-state tomography scheme. Finally, a classical post-processing step, formulated as a semidefinite program projecting onto the set of CPTP maps, returns a channel estimate Λ̂ satisfying ‖Λ̂-Λ‖_◇≤ε with high probability.

fundamentals.title: Operator structure of power corrections and anomalous scaling in energy correlators
fundamentals.abstract: Energy correlators offer a clean probe of quantum chromodynamics, serving as an ideal laboratory to rigorously investigate non-perturbative power corrections. The recent discovery that linear corrections exhibit a universal anomalous scaling points to a deep, underlying theoretical structure. We uncover the quantum field-theoretic origin of this phenomenon in the energy-energy correlator using light-ray operators. Through an explicit loop calculation, we derive the one-loop anomalous dimension, revealing that the dijet operator must be combined with a specific triple-jet component. This provides a first-principles framework that connects operator theory with high-precision collider phenomenology.

fundamentals.title: Unified theory of quartz tuning fork resonators
fundamentals.abstract: Quartz tuning forks, functioning as electrically driven piezoelectric resonators, have long served as exceptionally stable and widely adopted timing references in diverse domains of research and industry. Yet, experimentally measured electrical resonance spectra often exhibit resonance evolutions that remain unexplained within existing theoretical descriptions. Here we develop a unified continuum electromechanical modal framework that integrates piezoelectric electrodynamics, variational structural dynamics, and symmetry-selected electromechanical observability. Our theory shows quantitative agreement with experimental results, demonstrating that electrical observability emerges not from the underlying mechanical eigenmodes alone. The resulting framework unifies conventional coupled-oscillator, equivalent-circuit, and continuum descriptions within a single first-principles theory and provides a rigorous basis for precision electromechanical characterization.

fundamentals.title: Phase transition in a dryland shrub–grass ecosystem: Emergence through local trade-offs
fundamentals.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
fundamentals.abstract: Ecosystems are complex adaptive systems in which local interactions among individuals shape macroscopic phenomena such as pattern formation, multistability, and critical transitions. However, how such bottom-up interactions govern emergent behaviors and system-level complexity remains a central challenge in ecology. Phase transition theory, a classic paradigm in physics, links local interaction rules to emergent changes in macroscopic system states, offering a formal language for understanding cross-scale dynamics. Here we unite this theory with empirical evidence from dryland shrub-grass ecosystems and show that these systems exhibit three hallmarks of phase transitions. First, abrupt shifts separate different phases of deserts, shrublands, and grasslands. Second, shrublands and grasslands self-organize into Turing-like phase patterns, contrasting with homogeneous deserts. Third, special phenomena emerge near-transition threshold, including patch enlargement and abrupt decline at desert-vegetation interface, and fairy circles within the shrub-grass transition zone. Using a cellular automaton model built on a fundamental trade-off between extensive and intensive resource foraging strategies (EI trade-off), we show how kernels encoding local trade-offs integrate these seemingly disparate phenomena within a unified phase transition framework. Moreover, this EI trade-off was empirically validated through analyses of plant functional traits and spatial patterns of plant patches. These findings illustrate that dryland ecosystem dynamics reflect universal self-organization principles. Our work establishes phase-transition theory as a powerful framework for understanding, predicting, and managing complexity in dryland ecosystems, which advances the integration of complexity…

fundamentals.title: The Gopakumar--Vafa finiteness conjecture
fundamentals.abstract: The Gopakumar--Vafa conjecture predicts that the BPS invariants of a symplectic 6-manifold, defined in terms of the Gromov--Witten invariants, are integers and all but finitely many vanish in every homology class. The integrality part of this conjecture was proved earlier by Ionel and Parker. This article proves the finiteness part. The proof relies on a modification of Ionel and Parker's cluster formalism using results from geometric measure theory.

fundamentals.title: Microscopic theory of phonon polaritons and long-wavelength dielectric response
fundamentals.abstract: We present a first-principles approach for calculating phonon-polariton dispersion relations. In this approach, phonon-photon interaction is described by quantization of a Hamiltonian that describes harmonic lattice vibrations coupled with the electromagnetic field inside the material. All Hamiltonian parameters are obtained from first-principles calculations, with diagonalization leading to non-interacting polariton quasiparticles. This method naturally includes retardation effects and resolves non-analytical behavior and ambiguities in phonon frequencies at the Brillouin zone center, especially in non-cubic and optically anisotropic materials. Furthermore, by incorporating higher-order terms in the Hamiltonian, we also account for quasiparticle interactions and spectral broadening. Specifically, we show how anharmonic effects in phonon polaritons lead to a dielectric response that challenges traditional models. The accuracy and consequences of the approach are demonstrated on GaP and GaN as harmonic test systems and PbTe and β-Ga₂O₃ as anharmonic test systems.

fundamentals.title: Sound propagation in striped supersolid gases at zero temperature
fundamentals.abstract: The role of dimensionality in the identification of sound modes in many-body systems characterized by the spontaneous breaking of translational symmetry is a topic of high interdisciplinary interest in both classical and quantum systems. The emergence of stripes in superfluids is a particularly interesting example where the dimensionality of the system differs from the one of the crystal phase. Here we present a unified hydrodynamic approach for the sound propagation in the stripe phase realized in ultracold dipolar and spin-orbit-coupled Bose gases at zero temperature. Despite the deep difference of the two platforms at a microscopic level, a similar hydrodynamic description can be formulated at a macroscopic level. The main difference between the two platforms is the lack of Galilean invariance in the spin-orbit case, resulting in a different identification of the normal (non-superfluid) component of the density. In both cases the spectrum comprises two sounds, reflecting the spontaneous breaking of the U(1) and translational symmetries. Both sounds exhibit an anisotropic behavior. A comparison with the first and second sounds of the smectic-A liquid crystal is also presented.

fundamentals.title: High-dimensional families of holomorphic curves and three-dimensional energy surfaces
fundamentals.abstract: Let H: R⁴ → R be any smooth function. This article introduces some arguments for extracting dynamical information about the Hamiltonian flow of H from high-dimensional families of closed holomorphic curves. We work in a very general setting, without imposing convexity or contact-type assumptions. For any compact regular level set Y, we prove that the Hamiltonian flow admits an infinite family of pairwise distinct, proper, compact invariant subsets whose union is dense in Y. This is a generalization of the Fish--Hofer theorem, which showed that Y has at least one proper compact invariant subset. We then establish a global Le Calvez--Yoccoz property for almost every compact regular level set Y: any compact invariant subset containing all closed orbits is either equal to Y or is not locally maximal. Next, we prove quantitative versions, in four dimensions, of the celebrated almost-existence theorem for Hamiltonian systems; such questions have been open for general Hamiltonians since the late 1980s. We prove that almost every compact regular level set of H contains at least two closed orbits, a sharp lower bound. Under explicit and C^∞-generic conditions on H, we prove almost-existence of infinitely many closed orbits.

fundamentals.title: The Huang–Yang conjecture for the low-density Fermi gas
fundamentals.abstract: Our work establishes a three-term asymptotic expansion of the ground state energy of a dilute gas of spin 1/2 1 / 2 fermions with repulsive short-range interactions, validating a formula predicted by Huang and Yang in 1957. The formula is universal in the sense that it holds for a large class of interaction potentials and depends on those only via their scattering length. We have recently proved an upper bound on the ground state energy of the desired form, and the present work completes the program by proving the matching lower bound.
